notDoing.title: Four things you won't find here.
notDoing.subtitle: Worth saying before you ask, because the industry is full of all four.

items.title: Accessibility overlays and widgets
items.description: That floating button promising to fix everything with one line of script. It doesn't touch the code, it hides the problem, and in the United States there are lawsuits against sites that had one installed. If you have one, I'll tell you to remove it.

items.title: Conformance seals and certificates
items.description: Neither Law 11/2023 nor RD 1112/2018 provides for an official seal that anyone can issue you. What does exist is the accessibility statement or information that you publish and that you answer for. That I do deliver, written and ready.

items.title: Open-ended retainers with no scope
items.description: A monthly fee nobody can define ends up being a monthly fee that covers nothing. Everything on this page has a written scope and a fixed price before we start.

items.title: Automated-only audits
items.description: Tools find some of the problems, never all of them: they catch contrast, but not focus getting lost halfway through your form, nor a screen reader announcing your buy button as “empty link”. That only shows up navigating by hand. An axe report exported to PDF is not an audit.

items.question: How does billing work?
items.answer: 50% on confirmation and 50% on delivery. Formal invoice with VAT, valid for deduction. Ongoing compliance is billed monthly in arrears.

items.question: What is the difference between the express diagnosis and the audit?
items.answer: Depth, and what you take away. The diagnosis walks your homepage and up to three journeys along their main path and gives you the 10 findings costing you most: it answers "do I have a problem, and how big?". The audit evaluates the 50 WCAG 2.1 AA criteria over a documented sample, audits every complete process including its error states, and delivers the remediation plan and the compliance document the law requires: it answers "what am I missing, and how do I close it?". That is why one costs €290 and the other from €1,200.

items.question: Can I book remediation without the audit?
items.answer: If you bring me a recent and sufficiently detailed accessibility report, yes. If you don't have one, the audit is the prior step: you can't seriously fix what hasn't been diagnosed.

items.question: How do I know which tier my site falls into?
items.answer: By what people can do on it. If it only informs and receives enquiries, Essential. If people can buy, book or request an appointment, Commercial. If there are several of those processes or a private area with login, a fixed quote within 24 hours. I verify the size in your sitemap — you don't have to count pages.

items.question: Do you work with my in-house team or my agency?
items.answer: Yes, and that's the most common setup. The report is written so any technical profile can act on it directly. If you'd rather they apply it, that's fine: I audit, and then I review the result.

items.question: What if you miss a finding?
items.answer: I fix it at no additional cost within 60 days of delivering the report.

hero.label: WEB DEVELOPER • WEB ACCESSIBILITY SPECIALIST
hero.title: There are people trying to buy from you

hero.subtitle: A button the screen reader announces as “empty link”. A form nobody can complete by keyboard. Text that never quite gets read. These aren't technical details: they're orders walking away without you ever hearing about it. I audit and fix websites against WCAG 2.1 AA and Spain's Law 11/2023.

context.title: Before it's a legal problem, it's a revenue problem.

about.label: ABOUT ME
about.title: I was solving problems before I knew how to code
about.text_1: In the factory, I was already doing the same thing I do now: looking at a process, finding what doesn't work and imagining how to make it better. The difference is that before I thought about it and now I build it.
about.text_2: I studied Engineering in Topography — a career of measuring, calculating and being precise. I worked as a laborer in factories — where you see how things really work, not just the theory. And one day I discovered that web development allowed me to combine both things: technical precision and practical problem-solving.
about.text_3: Today my focus is on web accessibility. Laws have changed, websites haven't. There are thousands of companies required to comply with regulations that almost no one understands, with serious fines and real deadlines. And that's exactly the type of problem I've been solving my whole life: seeing how something should work and making it work.

problem.title: First you lose customers. The fine comes later.
problem.subtitle: Since 28 June 2025, Spain's Law 11/2023 has required thousands of companies to have an accessible website, and the vast majority don't. But the problem didn't start there: every barrier on your site is someone who doesn't finish buying.

risks.title: Customers who leave without telling you
risks.description: Only 8 in 100 shoppers with access needs contact the site owner when something doesn't work for them (Click-Away Pound, United Kingdom, 2019). The other 92 leave and buy from a competitor. In your analytics that just looks like another bounce.

risks.title: Real fines
risks.description: The penalty regime of RDL 1/2013, which Law 11/2023 refers to, is already in force. Failing accessibility requirements is a serious infringement, and repeat offences can escalate to very serious.

risks.title: Public procurement
risks.description: Spanish public procurement already requires accessibility criteria in technical specifications. If you work with the public sector, or want to, a conformant website stops being a nice-to-have and becomes a written requirement.

problem.closing: Auditing your site isn't a compliance whim. It's about no longer losing customers who had already chosen you — and clearing the legal risk while you're at it.

whoMustComply.title: Does this apply to you?
whoMustComply.subtitle: Not all websites are obligated equally. Spain's Law 11/2023 and RD 193/2023 define three groups with different deadlines. These are.

groups.headline: If you sell online or run digital services for consumers, you are already obligated.
groups.body: Ecommerce of any size. Online banking. Hotels with online booking. Airlines, rail, sea carriers. Telecom operators. Streaming platforms. Electricity, gas and water utilities. Online education platforms. Online travel agencies and tour operators.
groups.note: Exception: micro-enterprises (under 10 employees AND under €2M revenue) that only provide services without product sales.

groups.headline: If your sector runs a public-facing website, you're up in 2029.
groups.body: Clinics and healthcare services with online booking. Restaurants with online orders or bookings. Academies and training. Cultural, sports companies and museums with online sales. Mid-sized real estate. Financial services and insurance.
groups.note: Getting ahead now is a competitive advantage: most of your sector will only comply at the last minute.

groups.headline: If you receive public funds, the obligation is now, with no grace period.
groups.body: Spain's Kit Digital, EU funds, regional grants, contracts with the public sector. The Accessibility Review Report (IRA) is already required. Without compliance, risk of fund refund.

whoMustComply.closing: If you don't fit any of the three groups, you probably don't need this audit right now. If you fit at least one, you do.

process.title: 5 phases. 7 days. Zero improvisation.

steps.title: Manual and technical evaluation

steps.clientInput: What I need from you: nothing. If something critical comes up, I'll let you know right away.

steps.title: Report writing and remediation plan
steps.description: I structure all findings in the final document: executive summary, catalog by criterion, prioritized plan with estimated hours, accessibility statement. I review twice before delivering.
steps.clientInput: What I need from you: nothing. What I need from myself: rigor.

faq.title: What people usually ask before hiring.

items.question: How long does the audit take exactly?
items.answer: 5-7 business days from the initial briefing. Most audits I deliver in 5. Larger sites can require up to 7.

items.question: Are you going to audit every page on my website?
items.answer: No, and I shouldn't. The W3C reference methodology, WCAG-EM 2.0, evaluates the conformance of a whole site from a representative sample: common views, one instance of each template, every technology you rely on, and an additional 10% picked at random to catch what a targeted selection would miss. Processes — buying, booking, signing up — are audited in full, start to finish, including their error states. The report lists every single URL evaluated, so the sample is verifiable and reproducible.

items.question: How do I know which tier I fall into?
items.answer: By what people can do on your site, not by its size. If your site informs and people contact you, that's the Essential tier: €1,200. If people can buy, book or request an appointment, that's Commercial: €2,200. If there are several of those processes or a private area with login, you get a fixed quote within 24 hours. I check the page count in your sitemap myself — you don't have to count anything.

items.question: What is the difference between the express diagnosis and the audit?
items.answer: Depth, and what you take away. The diagnosis walks your homepage and up to three journeys along their main path and gives you the 10 findings costing you most: it answers "do I have a problem, and how big?". The audit evaluates the 50 WCAG 2.1 AA criteria over a documented sample, audits every complete process including its error states, and delivers the remediation plan and the compliance document the law requires: it answers "what am I missing, and how do I close it?". That is why one costs €290 and the other from €1,200.

items.question: Does the audit include implementing the corrections?
items.answer: No. The audit is only the diagnosis: I deliver the full report with every finding and the remediation plan. Implementation is optional, with a separate quote, and only if you decide I do it.

items.question: Do I need anything ready before starting?
items.answer: Just access to your site (if it has private areas or staging). If you don't have any of that, even better: the audit is faster.

items.question: Can I apply the corrections myself?
items.answer: Yes. The report is designed so your technical team can act on it directly. If you have an in-house developer or agency, you hand them the document and they apply it.

items.question: Does this fulfill the legal requirement of Law 11/2023?
items.answer: Yes. The audit includes the accessibility statement drafted under RD 1112/2018, ready to publish on your site. It meets the formal evaluation requirement of the regulation.

items.question: How is it invoiced?
items.answer: 50% at confirmation of the audit start, 50% at report delivery. Formal invoice with VAT, valid for deduction.

items.question: What if your audit misses something and I get reported later?
items.answer: I work with WCAG 2.1 AA + EN 301549 methodology. It's the legal standard in Spain. If a finding slips and appears later, I fix it at no additional cost within 60 days after report delivery.
